newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: EU ruling lifts Telecel, hurts PT.
newsitem.headline: EU ruling lifts Telecel, hurts PT.

text.p: A European Commission ruling that Portugal should allow GSM operators to use "alternative infrastructure" immediately pushed up shares of mobile phone operator Telecel on Thursday and weighed on Portugal Telecom, analysts said.
"In the future, Telecel won't have to lease lines from PT any more," said Jose Freire of Espirito Santo Research.
"They will be able to set up their own lines and costs will drop drastically; or PT will drop the rates at which it offers land lines to them," he said.
"This news will help Telecel because 20 percent of its turnover is land costs, although the impact on PT's business is much less."
Joao Vermelho, analyst with Lisbon broker Central Investimentos, said: "PT will come under pressure to reduce the rates at which it provides lines to Telecel."
Mark Howard of Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Cascais said: "PT is going to have to offer Telecel a really good deal to maintain their relationship."
Telecel shares stood at 13,300 escudos, up 254, in volume of 48,409 on Lisbon bourse at 1507 GMT. Portugal Telecom shares fell 37 escudos to 6,002 in volume of 211,707.

The Commission's announcement on Wednesday that Portugal could delay the liberalisation of its telecommunications markets until the beginning of 2000, two years after most other EU states must act, was expected in the market, analysts said.
The ruling that Portugal should open its market for direct international GSM mobile phone connections by January 1, 1999, also came as no surprise, they added.
Portugal asked to delay full liberalisation until January 1, 2000 to give PT time to reorganise and the government time to complete studies on "rebalancing" tariffs to bring them in line with costs.

Lisbon also asked to delay liberalisation of alternative infrastructure for three years beyond the EU deadline, saying PT earned about six percent of its revenues from providing leased circuits and immediate lifting of restrictions could lead to big revenue losses.

However, the Commission said such a long delay was not warranted since market growth would compensate for any potential revenue losses and the company could continue to develop its network during the runup to the 2000 deadline.
